title: Optimal Stop Spacing and Service Frequency in Public Transport Networks: A Continuous Fixed-Point Approach
text:
Overview & Contribution
Removing stops shortens vehicle cycles but lengthens the walk to a stop. Under a fixed operating budget, the released cycle time can fund a higher frequency. This paper formulates the joint stop-spacing and frequency problem as a continuous program and solves it to global optimality.

Fixed point of closed-form blocks: For fixed frequencies, each segment has an independent spacing condition. For fixed spacings, line frequencies follow a generalized Mohring rule under the budget. Because the program is convex in the logarithms of spacing and frequency, the fixed point gives the global optimum. On a three-line instance it converges in six iterations and 0.009 seconds, whereas spatial branch-and-bound needs 527,000 nodes and 17 seconds.
Health value of walking: Valuing the health benefit of walking shifts the optimal spacing upward. Omitting it understates the Danish single-line optimum by 13%.
Copenhagen application: For 450 segments on 172 bus lines, the method solves in milliseconds. Under the existing bus budget, demand-weighted spacing rises from 0.51 to 0.57 km and frequency from 7.3 to 9.2 trips per hour, and frequency moves toward the central network.

title: Optimal Stop Spacing and Service Frequency in Public Transport Networks: A Continuous Fixed-Point Approach
text:
Abstract
Removing stops shortens vehicle cycles but lengthens passenger access. Under a fixed operating budget, the released cycle time can fund higher frequency. We formulate the joint spacing–frequency problem as a continuous programme and solve it by a fixed point between two closed-form blocks. For fixed frequencies, each segment has an independent spacing condition. For fixed spacings, line frequencies follow a generalised Mohring rule under a fixed budget. The programme is convex in the logarithms of spacing and frequency, so the fixed point gives the global optimum. On a controlled three-line instance it reaches this optimum in six iterations and 0.009 seconds, whereas spatial branch-and-bound requires 527 thousand nodes and 17 seconds. The model yields an interior welfare optimum, and we bound the loss from rounding the continuous spacing to a whole number of stops. Health valuation shifts optimal spacing upward, and omitting it understates the Danish single-line optimum by 13%. We also apply the method to 450 segments on 172 bus lines in Copenhagen, where it solves in milliseconds. Under the existing bus budget, demand-weighted spacing rises from 0.51 to 0.57 km and frequency from 7.3 to 9.2 trips per hour. With walking valued at 7.5 DKK/km for its health benefit, optimal spacing is 11% wider than the operated design. Without that value it is slightly tighter. The larger change is that frequency moves toward the central network and away from the outer lines.

title: From Fractions to Individuals: Information-Theoretic Integerization for Population Synthesis
text:
Overview & Contribution
Population synthesis produces large, sparse contingency tables with fractional counts, which must be converted to whole persons before an agent-based model can use them. This paper treats integerization as information-theoretic inference instead of sampling.

KL-closest integer table: Among all integer tables consistent with the margins, the method selects the one closest in Kullback–Leibler divergence to the fractional IPF solution, with each cell set to its floor or its ceiling.
Deterministic algorithm: The solution requires two sparse IPF runs and a largest-remainder allocation, so it scales as IPF itself. Identical inputs give identical outputs, and there is no sampling variance.
Empirical results: For 98 Danish municipalities with 635,000 joint cells, the integer table overlaps 98.4% with the fractional solution, against 92.1% for multinomial sampling. An extension to 397 million cells is integerized in 16 minutes.

title: From Fractions to Individuals: Information-Theoretic Integerization for Population Synthesis
text:
Abstract
High-dimensional population synthesis produces sparse contingency tables with many fractional counts that must be integerized for agent-based models. Standard sampling approaches introduce stochastic noise. We recast integerization as an information-theoretic inference problem: among all integer tables consistent with the margins, select the one closest to the fractional IPF solution in Kullback–Leibler divergence. We restrict the search to integerizations that assign each cell either its floor or ceiling value, which yields a simple two-step algorithm that is reproducible and efficient. Applied to 98 Danish municipalities with 635,000 joint cells across socio-economic groups, the integer table overlaps 98.4% with the fractional IPF solution, versus 92.1% for multinomial sampling. Identical inputs produce identical outputs, eliminating sampling variance. Primary margins are exact; secondary margins may carry small residuals. The method replaces traditional sampling-based integerization with deterministic inference that yields a single, stable, reproducible solution. The algorithm consists of two sparse IPF runs and a largest-remainder allocation, so it scales as IPF itself; an extension to 397 million cells is integerized in 16 minutes.

title: Plug-in electric vehicle adoption in Europe: A cross-country analysis of preferences and willingness-to-pay in six markets
text:
Overview & Contribution
The demand for battery electric vehicles (BEVs) and plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs) has grown across Europe, but at different rates. This paper compares preferences for both across six European markets at different stages of adoption: the Czech Republic, Denmark, Germany, Ireland, Italy and Spain.

Harmonized survey: Stated preference data from a harmonized European survey with 1,000 respondents per country give consistent and comparable data. Revealed preference data of this kind are not available across the six countries.
Mixed logit with country effects: Mixed logit models with country-specific effects give willingness-to-pay measures for vehicle attributes and preferences for fuel types across population segments.
Empirical findings: Preferences for BEVs and PHEVs are most negative in the Czech Republic and most positive in Denmark, Italy and Spain. The gap between home and apartment dwellers is largest in Germany, where the ranking depends on access to home charging. The countries therefore face different barriers to adoption.

title: Plug-in electric vehicle adoption in Europe: A cross-country analysis of preferences and willingness-to-pay in six markets
text:
Abstract
The demand for battery electric vehicles (BEVs) and plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs) has increased across Europe, but at very different rates. Most existing studies focus on single countries, making it challenging to compare preferences and identify why adoption differs. In this paper, we compare preferences for BEVs and PHEVs across six European markets with highly varying adoption levels: the Czech Republic, Denmark, Germany, Ireland, Italy, and Spain.
We estimate mixed logit models with country-specific effects using stated preference data from a harmonised European survey with 1,000 respondents per country. The models are used to calculate willingness-to-pay measures for vehicle attributes and quantify preferences for fuel types across population segments. We observe large differences in preferences between home and apartment dwellers across countries, with the gap particularly pronounced in Germany. Preferences related to both BEVs and PHEVs are most negative in the Czech Republic, and most positive in Denmark, Italy, and Spain. For Germany, the relative ranking is highly dependent on access to home charging. These results indicate that countries face different barriers to electric vehicle adoption. In some cases, improving charging access and economic incentives may be sufficient, while in others, barriers related to attitudes and awareness may require targeted measures beyond infrastructure and pricing.

title: Beyond Box-Cox: A diffusion-inspired functional framework for nonlinear demand and discrete choice modeling
text:
Overview & Contribution
Standard linear-in-attributes and Box–Cox utility specifications struggle when travel cost or distance spans wide ranges, often producing unrealistic tail elasticities or requiring ad-hoc spline knots. This paper introduces a diffusion-inspired functional family for nonlinear demand and discrete choice models that naturally captures cost damping, saturation, and distance-decay profiles with parsimonious parameters and well-behaved derivatives.

title: Modelling transport market adaptation using synthetic pseudo-panels: Application to e-bike diffusion
text:
Overview & Contribution
New transport technologies often spread first in small population segments, where repeated cross-sectional surveys contain too few observations to follow adoption over time. This paper introduces a synthetic pseudo-panel (SPP) approach and applies it to ten years of e-bike adoption in Denmark.

Synthetic pseudo-panel: A conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) learns the conditional distribution of the survey variables. This allows consistent adoption trajectories to be reconstructed for detailed segments that the raw data cover only sparsely.
Decomposition of mileage: The reconstructed trajectories decompose changes in mileage and show how travel is reallocated between modes as preferences shift over time.
Empirical findings: Adoption is strongest in suburban areas and city centers and lags in rural regions. Women and older adults are leading adopters and mainly replace bicycle trips, and there is evidence of induced demand among previously non-travelling individuals.

title: Modelling transport market adaptation using synthetic pseudo-panels: Application to e-bike diffusion
text:
Abstract
Emerging transport technologies often diffuse through niche segments, where survey-based methods struggle to capture adoption dynamics due to limited sample sizes. To address this, we introduce a synthetic pseudo-panel (SPP) framework employing conditional variational autoencoders (CVAE) to reconstruct consistent adoption trajectories from repeated cross-sectional data. Applied to e-bike adoption in Denmark over a ten-year period, the framework enables decomposition of mileage changes and reveals modal reallocation patterns through shifts in preference distributions over time. Results highlight distinct socio-demographic and geographic pathways, with early signals detectable before they appear in raw data. Adoption is strongest in suburban areas and city centres, while rural regions lag. Women and elderly adults emerge as leading adopters, primarily reallocating bicycle trips, though effects extend to other modes as well. Evidence of induced demand suggests e-bikes may enable mobility among previously non-travelling individuals. The framework is broadly applicable to domains characterised by gradual behavioural diffusion, including automated vehicles, electric mobility, and energy transitions.

title: Generational action-space dynamics over two decades: A continuity density-field perspective
text:
Overview & Contribution
This paper introduces a physics-inspired framework for analyzing how six birth cohorts reorganize their daily activity in space and time over two decades, using 18 survey years of Danish National Travel Survey data (2007–2024, N = 115,338 retained person-days).

Action-Space Continuity Field: Each survey wave defines a cohort-level action-space density field \rho_c(d, t; \tau) — the probability of being active at distance d from home at time of day t in period \tau.
Continuity Equation & Drift: Successive temporal snapshots are linked via an analogy to the fluid-mechanics continuity equation, extracting drift vectors, speed fields, and source/sink terms that characterize how spatial reach and out-of-home duration co-evolve.
Empirical Findings: Results reveal spatial expansion paired with reduced time away from home for cohorts born 1960–2000, predominantly temporal contraction for the oldest cohort, and spatial expansion at an almost unchanged away-time fraction for the youngest cohort.

text:
🟢 GitHub: jepperich69/ai-infrastructure (Public)
  ⚙️ Code bases & Algorithms
Modern quantitative research involves coordinating concurrent manuscripts, mathematical proofs, solver benchmarks, and co-author revisions. To maintain high scientific rigor and zero administrative drift across projects, I built AI_auto — a unified command-line and multi-agent infrastructure (helpi) connecting Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and Google Gemini around standardized project folders.

title: AI Research Infrastructure (AI_auto)
text:
Core Design Principles

Standalone Overleaf + GitHub Separation: Every paper project (Pub_*, Pro_*, PhD_*) isolates Overleaf_source/ as a direct Git remote to Overleaf (helpi 3 pull, helpi 4 push) while code/ is a separate Git repository pushed to GitHub (helpi 23).
Machine-Verified Mathematics (SymPy Gate): LLMs have no built-in symbolic engine and can make silent algebraic errors. Our infrastructure enforces a strict rule: every non-trivial algebraic derivation, Taylor expansion, moment derivation, and numerical calibration must be verified via executable SymPy scripts (_math_checks/) before entering a manuscript.
Multi-Agent Convergence Forum (helpi 25): Complex modeling questions, literature audits, and pre-submission referee stress-tests are debated in an automated multi-round Convergence Forum where agents adopt distinct adversarial roles (Critic, Advocate, Realist, and Moderator) against a shared blackboard state until convergence.
Routine Scientific Code Review (helpi 32): Before closing any session that modifies model code or empirical claims, an advisory review checks scientific correspondence between the paper’s equations and the code, verifies reuse of verified jr_optlib primitives, and audits numerical reproducibility.
Automated Communication Deliverables:

Technical One-Pagers (helpi 24): Boils a full manuscript down to a dense, self-contained 1-page A4 technical brief + 1-page equation/note supplement.
Beamer Slides & 3-Minute Video Decks (helpi 19): Generates structured presentation decks and 6-slide video briefs.
Website Sync (helpi 33): Publishes updated one-pagers, slides, 3-minute videos (via GitHub Releases), and repository status badges directly to this Quarto website.

Short Biography
Jeppe Rich is Professor at the Technical University of Denmark (DTU Management, Department of Technology, Management and Economics) specializing in large-scale transport modelling, optimization, and econometrics. Holding an M.Sc. in Mathematical Planning from the University of Aarhus (1995) and a Ph.D. from DTU (2001), he works across quantitative transportation science, including discrete choice and demand models, mixed-integer and stochastic optimization, population synthesis, charging infrastructure planning, freight electrification, and bicycle demand.
In March 2023, he was appointed Co-Editor-in-Chief and Founding Editor of the Elsevier journal Journal of Cycling and Micromobility Research, co-founded with Professor Eva Heinen. Throughout his career he has led numerous national and European transport modelling programmes, notably serving as chief designer for the Danish National Transport Model (LTM), a €7 million venture. He is the recipient of the 2025 Danish Transport Research Prize.
He collaborates closely with international academic partners (including TU Delft, NTNU, ETH Zurich, University of Leeds, KU, TUM, KTH, Tongji, Technion, and MIT) as well as ministries, public authorities, and the European Commission.

title: The Diverging Action-Space: Evolving Rhythms and Changing Habits in Daily Mobility
text:
Overview & Contribution
Using 18 years of Danish National Travel Survey data (115,338 weekday diaries), this paper examines whether the spatial and temporal structure of daily mobility has changed in an era of digitization, remote work and a pandemic, or whether people leave home less often but keep their patterns once they do.

Action-space representation: Each diary is represented as the distance from home over the 24-hour day. Spatial reach and temporal rhythm are therefore measured together, for five age groups.
Spatial expansion: The conditional envelope, which describes where people go when they travel, expands in every age group and significantly in three of them. The expansion is largest for adults aged 56–65 (+12.9%), and it is a long-run trend that was already present before 2019.
Temporal contraction: The share of the day spent away from home falls by 3.2–6.3% for the age groups below 56, mainly after 2019, and rises by 8.2% for those aged 56–65. All age groups shift their activities earlier in the day.

title: The Diverging Action-Space: Evolving Rhythms and Changing Habits in Daily Mobility
text:
Abstract
How much has daily mobility changed in an era of digitization, remote work, and a global pandemic? Using 18 years of Danish travel data (115,338 weekday diaries), we analyze daily action-spaces—the distance from home over time—across five age groups. We identify a two-regime structure. The conditional action-space envelope, which describes where people go when they travel, expands spatially in every age group, and significantly in three of them. The expansion is largest for pre-retirement adults (56–65, +12.9%), lies between +5.8% and +6.6% for the three age groups below 56, and is smallest and not significant for adults aged 66 and above (+2.9%). This expansion is a long-run trend that was already present before 2019. Temporal rhythms within the envelope remain stable. In contrast, the unconditional share of the day spent away from home moves in opposite directions on either side of age 56. It declines by 6.3% for 18–30, 6.2% for 31–55 and 3.2% for 10–17, whereas it increases by 8.2% for 56–65. For the groups below 56, this contraction is concentrated after 2019. Before then, their time away from home was rising for 10–17 and 31–55 and declining only slightly for 18–30. All age groups shift their activities earlier in the day and spend less of the evening away from home. The divergence between spatial expansion and temporal contraction therefore applies to the age groups below 56, and its temporal side is largely a development of the most recent survey periods.

title: Future environmental impacts of electric heavy-duty trucks
text:
Overview & Contribution
Battery-electric trucks are a main option for decarbonizing long-haul heavy-duty transport, but their life-cycle benefits depend on future electricity supply and vehicle technology. This paper performs a prospective life cycle assessment of 40-tonne diesel and battery-electric long-haul trucks for most countries and regions of the world, from 2025 to 2050.

Prospective technology: Changes in battery energy density, vehicle lightweighting and the regulatory gross vehicle weight allowance are represented explicitly, for several battery sizes.
Climate impacts: The life-cycle climate change impacts of battery-electric trucks fall substantially from 2025, mainly because the electricity system is decarbonized. By 2050 they are about 66–85% lower than those of diesel trucks across the regions analysed.
Other impact categories: Battery-electric trucks have higher impacts in several categories related to material production, although technological improvements reduce these over time.

title: Future environmental impacts of electric heavy-duty trucks
text:
Abstract
Battery-electric trucks (BETs) are a key option for decarbonizing long-haul heavy-duty transport, yet their life-cycle environmental benefits depend on future electricity supply and vehicle technology development. This study performs a prospective life cycle assessment of 40 tonne diesel and battery-electric long-haul trucks, modeled for most countries/regions in the world, from 2025 to 2050 and under different configurations of battery sizes. Prospective changes in battery gravimetric energy density, vehicle lightweighting, and regulatory gross vehicle weight allowances are represented explicitly. Results show that life-cycle climate change impacts of battery-electric trucks decrease substantially from 2025 onwards, driven primarily by electricity system decarbonization. Vehicle-side improvements provide additional reductions and narrow differences between battery-electric truck configurations with different driving ranges. While climate benefits are apparent, battery-electric trucks exhibit higher impacts in several other environmental impacts related to material production, though these are partially mitigated by technological improvements over time. By 2050, battery-electric trucks achieve life-cycle climate change emissions approximately 66–85% lower than those of diesel trucks across the analysed regions. Overall, the results highlight the dominant role of electricity system decarbonization in enabling these reductions, while vehicle technology improvements act as complementary enablers across regions and long-haul applications.

title: On the theoretical distribution of cost overruns: A lognormal baseline
text:
Overview & Contribution
Why do infrastructure cost overruns exhibit persistent right-skewness and systematic mean–median gaps? This paper develops a two-level stochastic framework separating within-project compounding from cross-project dependence:

Within-project multiplicative baseline: When project costs evolve through sequential proportional updates between baseline and completion, the cost ratio R = C_a / C_e converges under weak dependence toward a lognormal benchmark. Compounding alone generates a structural gap between mean and median cost ratios (\mathbb{E}[R] = \exp(\mu + \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2) > \exp(\mu) = \mathrm{Med}[R]), even when individual stage updates have zero log-drift.
Portfolio aggregation & correlation (Proposition 1): Under cross-project independence, portfolio aggregation restores asymptotic symmetry by the Central Limit Theorem. Persistent right-skewness at the portfolio level is therefore a mathematical diagnostic of correlated shocks (shared macro, regulatory, or factor exposures across projects in a portfolio).
Empirical calibration: The framework is illustrated across international transport infrastructure datasets (Flyvbjerg), Swedish stage-split transport projects (Eliasson: early plan-to-start stage vs. late start-to-completion stage), and IT project portfolios (Flyvbjerg & Budzier, N = 4,677).


Key takeaway: Part of what is commonly attributed purely to behavioral “optimism bias” reflects the structural mathematics of multiplicative compounding combined with correlated portfolio shocks.

title: Recasting Mixed-Integer Programs as Probability Problems
text:
Overview & Contribution
A mixed-integer solver reports whether a solution is optimal, but not how stable it is, how many near-optimal alternatives exist, or how uncertain the objective is. This paper introduces Probabilistic MIP (PMIP), which treats the optimization process itself as a source of statistical information.

Entropy annealing: An entropy term is added to the relaxation, and the temperature is lowered gradually. Each stage defines a Boltzmann-like probability measure over feasible integer solutions. Dual-guided rounding converts the relaxation to integer solutions, and a short Metropolis–Hastings swap-and-repair step refines them.
Single-run uncertainty: From one annealing trajectory, the method derives the mean, the variance and credible intervals of the objective without repeated solver calls. It runs in polynomial time, with little overhead relative to a standard hybrid solve.
Applications: In transportation and set-cover problems, the confidence limits bracket the true optimum while the method keeps its computational scalability.

title: Recasting Mixed-Integer Programs as Probability Problems
text:
Abstract
This paper introduces a rapid, information-theoretic framework for mixed-integer optimization that enables simultaneous assessment of solution quality and uncertainty. By embedding an entropy term into the relaxation and gradually annealing the temperature, we transform a deterministic solver into a distributional one, where each annealing stage defines a Boltzmann-like probability measure over feasible integer solutions. The continuous relaxation is converted to integer solutions via dual-guided rounding; in the presence of total unimodularity, this step reduces to solving a standard linear program. From this annealing trajectory, we derive single-run estimates of the mean, variance, and credible intervals of the objective function without repeated solver calls. The method, termed PMIP, operates in polynomial time and adds minimal runtime overhead relative to a standard hybrid solve. It provides a self-consistent answer to the questions “how good is good?” and “how uncertain is uncertain?”, linking heuristic optimality to the statistical structure of the near-optimal solution space. Applications to transportation and set-cover problems show that the resulting confidence limits reliably bracket the true optimum while preserving computational scalability.

title: RICH: A Rapid Information-Theoretic Hybrid Algorithm for Mixed-Integer Optimization
text:
Overview & Contribution
Large mixed-integer programs force a choice between exact methods, which guarantee optimality but scale poorly, and heuristics, which scale well but give up solution quality and guarantees. This paper presents RICH, a hybrid method that combines an entropy-regularized relaxation with structured integerization.

Entropy-regularized relaxation: The linear relaxation is replaced by an entropy-regularized convex program, which is solved by Sinkhorn iterations or iterative proportional fitting (IPF) in near-linear time.
KL rounding: Integer solutions are recovered by minimum Kullback–Leibler divergence rounding. For transportation and assignment problems the method recovers exact optimal solutions, and for population synthesis it has a zero integrality gap on totally unimodular systems.
Computational results: Population synthesis reaches exact marginals in under 2 seconds for 160×160 tables, and transportation problems are solved optimally in under 1 second for 300×300 instances. For set covering from 100×3,000 to 300×5,000, the hybrid reaches good feasible solutions in about 2 seconds, and its advantage over time-limited MIP grows with the instance size.

title: RICH: A Rapid Information-Theoretic Hybrid Algorithm for Mixed-Integer Optimization
text:
Abstract
We present a method for approximating solutions to large-scale mixed-integer programs by combining: (i) entropy-regularized linear relaxation solved via Sinkhorn iterations, and (ii) structured integerization via minimum Kullback–Leibler divergence rounding. The approach leverages information-theoretic projections for scalability while producing high-quality solutions through entropy-aware rounding. The method applies to a host of problems, including transport, network flows, facility location, set covering, and population synthesis. For lattice polytopes (e.g., transportation and assignment), it recovers exact optimal solutions. For population synthesis, it achieves zero integrality gap on totally unimodular systems and provably bounded deviations for more complex non-TU linked-constraint cases. For general set covering, it provides high-quality approximate solutions with the classical logarithmic approximation guarantee. We evaluate on three representative problem classes at varying scales: (i) population synthesis achieving exact marginals in under 2 s for 160×160 tables, (ii) transportation problems solved optimally in under 1 s for 300×300 instances, and (iii) synthetic set covering across three scales (100×3000 to 300×5000), where the hybrid reaches high-quality feasible solutions within about 2 s and its advantage over time-limited MIP becomes more pronounced as instance size grows, with the larger scales retaining a positive gap advantage throughout a 30 s horizon. The method bridges information geometry and combinatorial optimization, providing a scalable, theoretically grounded alternative to traditional MIP heuristics.

Overview: This interactive model is a calibrated fast surrogate of the Danish National Transport Model (LTM 2.3, Rich 2022), rebased to 2023 using Danish National Travel Survey (TU 0624v1), TERESA 6.21 values of time, TØE 2.2 vehicle operating costs, and distance-dependent public transport fare profiles (Argyros, Jensen & Rich, 2026; Rich & Fox, 2024). The calculator is available in Danish and English; switch language in the app header.

100% browser-based: All calibration, scenario evaluation, and rule-of-half distributional welfare calculations run locally in your browser via engine2.js.
Custom workbooks: You can save scenarios locally or upload a modified .xlsx input workbook directly inside the interface to recalibrate in ~8 seconds.
